t.2.82.8: At the proper time, the scorcher of foes was praised by bards and by many sūtas and māgadhas with fitting songs and hymns of praise.
t.2.82.7: He who was always awakened by the resounding of songs and instruments, by the tinkling of fine ornaments, and by the excellent sounds of the mṛdaṅga drums.
t.2.82.5: Always in the towering chambers atop palaces and in turreted pavilions, on floors of gold and silver graced with the finest spreads and carpets,
t.2.82.6: In those mansions bright with heaps of flowers, fragrant with sandalwood and aloe, gleaming like white clouds, and echoing with the cries of flocks of parrots,
t.2.82.11: And Sītā too, the lovely daughter of the king of Videha, the beloved daughter-in-law of Daśaratha, lay upon the bare ground.
t.2.82.10: Surely no deity whatsoever is mightier than Time, since he, Rāma the son of Daśaratha, should have to lie like this upon the ground.
t.2.82.12: This is my brother's bed; here indeed, on the hard bare ground, he tossed and turned, and all the grass has been crushed by his limbs.
t.2.82.13: I think that Sītā slept on this bed then with her ornaments still on, for here and there little specks of gold are seen clinging to it.
t.2.82.14: Clearly Sītā's upper garment caught here at that time, for these silken threads that clung here are plainly visible.
t.2.82.15: I think her husband's bed must be a comfortable one, since the young and pitiable Maithilī, delicate though she is, feels no hardship.
t.2.82.16: Born into a family of universal sovereigns, bringer of happiness to all the world and beloved of all the world, he has given up the kingdom, dear and unsurpassed.
t.2.82.18: Fortunate indeed is Vaidehī, who followed her husband into the forest; all of us are left in doubt and peril, bereft of that great-souled one.
t.2.82.17: How could Rāghava, dark as the blue lotus, red-eyed and pleasing to behold, who was meant to enjoy happiness and has now come to merit sorrow, have lain sleeping on the bare ground?
t.2.82.19: With Daśaratha gone to heaven and Rāma having taken refuge in the forest, the earth seems to me like a ship without a helmsman, as though it were empty.
t.2.82.20: No one would covet, even in his mind, the earth protected by the might of his arms, even while he dwells in the forest.
t.2.82.21: The royal capital, its ramparts and guard-posts deserted, its horses and elephants unrestrained, its city gates thrown open, lying unprotected.
t.2.82.23: From this day forth I shall sleep on the bare ground or on grass, always living on fruits and roots and wearing matted locks and garments of bark.
t.2.82.22: Though her forces are dispirited, though she is depleted, in a precarious state and unprotected, enemies do not covet her, as men shun food that has been poisoned.
t.2.82.24: For his sake I shall dwell happily in the forest for the time that remains; once I have taken that promise upon myself, it shall not prove false for him.
t.2.82.26: The twice-born will consecrate Kākutstha in Ayodhyā. May the gods make this heart's desire of mine come true!
t.2.82.25: While I dwell there for my brother's sake, Śatrughna will dwell with me, and the noble one, together with Lakṣmaṇa, will protect Ayodhyā.
t.2.82.27: If, though I myself propitiate him in many ways with my head bowed low, he will not consent, then I shall follow Rāghava and dwell with him in the forest for a long time; he ought not to disregard me.
t.2.82.9: This is unbelievable in the world; it does not seem true to me. My mind is truly bewildered; my thought is that this is a dream.
t.2.82.1: Having heard all that precise account, Bharata, together with his ministers, came to the foot of the iṅgudī tree and gazed upon that bed of Rāma.
t.2.82.2: He said to all the mothers: "Here the night was spent lying on the ground by that great-souled one; this is what was pressed down by him."
t.2.82.3: Rāma, begotten by Daśaratha, the illustrious and wise king born of an illustrious lineage, ought not to sleep upon the bare earth.
t.2.82.4: Having once slept upon a heap of the finest coverlets, spread over with an antelope skin, how does that tiger among men now lie upon the bare ground?
